mcqs.question: Why do most language standard libraries back their stack/queue/deque types with a resizable array rather than a linked list?
options: Contiguous, cache-friendly memory access, at the cost of occasional amortized O(1) resizing, usually beats a linked list's pointer overhead and poor locality
Linked lists cannot support push and pop operations
Arrays use more memory per element than linked lists
A resizable array has better worst-case time per single operation than a linked list
mcqs.explanation: The practical win is memory locality: contiguous array storage lets the CPU prefetch effectively, while list nodes scatter across memory and each pointer costs extra bytes. Linked lists support push/pop fine, and a single array resize is actually O(n) in the worst case — it's the amortized cost across many operations that ends up O(1), not every individual operation.

mcqs.question: Why is returning `None` from an empty-stack `pop()` a risky design in general-purpose stack code?
options: It makes pop run in O(n) instead of O(1)
`None` may also be a legitimately stored value, making it impossible for calling code to distinguish "stack is empty" from "the top element happens to be None"
It's fine — None is always a safe sentinel for any stack
It causes the stack to silently grow instead of shrink
mcqs.explanation: If the stack can legitimately hold `None` as a stored value, using it as an empty-stack sentinel creates an unresolvable ambiguity for the caller. It has no effect on time complexity or growth direction — the concern is purely about correctly signaling an error condition rather than confusing it with valid data.

mcqs.question: An array-backed queue avoids shifting elements by just advancing a "front" index on dequeue instead of moving data. What problem does this alone still leave unsolved?
options: Dequeue becomes O(n) again
The space before the advancing front index is never reused, wasting array capacity over many enqueue/dequeue cycles
Enqueue can no longer be performed
The queue becomes a stack
mcqs.explanation: Advancing the front index avoids the O(n) shift, which is the main win — but the array slots before that index are simply abandoned, since nothing writes back into them, so a long-running queue can end up mostly empty while still holding its full original allocation. Enqueue still works, dequeue is genuinely O(1) with this change, and the FIFO ordering is unaffected — the queue doesn't turn into a stack.

mcqs.question: A problem statement says "undo the last five actions performed." Which structure does this describe, even though the word never appears?
options: A queue, because actions are processed in the order they occurred
A priority queue, because urgency determines order
A hash map, because actions need to be looked up by name
A stack, because "undo the last" means accessing the most recently added item first — last in, first out
mcqs.explanation: "Undo the last" is exactly a LIFO access pattern — the most recently performed action is the first one reversed — which is a stack regardless of whether the problem uses that word. It isn't ordered by arrival for processing (queue), doesn't involve priority ranking, and doesn't need key-based lookup.

mcqs.question: A queue is implemented as `queue.append(x)` for enqueue and `queue.pop(0)` for dequeue, using a plain dynamic-array list. What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing — both operations are O(1)
`append` is O(n) but `pop(0)` is O(1)
`pop(0)` is O(n) because every remaining element must shift down one slot, making the "queue" silently O(n) per dequeue
The queue will process elements in the wrong order
mcqs.explanation: A plain array-backed list is only cheap to pop from the end; removing from the front requires shifting every remaining element, an O(n) cost hidden behind what looks like a simple method call. `append` genuinely is O(1) amortized, and the FIFO ordering is correct — the problem is purely a hidden performance cost, not a logic bug.
